speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minster for Finance)
text: The Goods and Services Tax (Amendment) Bill 2024 makes amendments to address the issue of wrongful charging of Goods and Services Tax (GST) on fees charged by the Government and statutory bodies, excluding Town Councils, which I will refer to collectively as "Government fees".

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minster for Finance)
text: Such regulatory fees should not be subject to GST as they are imposed for the purposes of control and regulation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minster for Finance)
text: In contrast, fees for provision of services, such as for the rental of public sports facilities, should be subject to GST.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minster for Finance)
text: This approach ensures parity in tax treatment, where services that can potentially be provided by, or outsourced to the private or non-Government sector, are subject to GST.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minster for Finance)
text: Some countries which levy GST also adopt similar principles.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minster for Finance)
text: We have, thus far, left it to agencies to self-assess and determine what constitutes a regulatory fee, with guidance provided through Government circulars.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minster for Finance)
text: However, agencies may not always be clear where to draw the line.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minster for Finance)
text: This is not ideal and can give rise to wrongful charging of GST, as was the case for the 18 fees.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minster for Finance)
text: This is why, in response to several Members' earlier Parliamentary Questions on how the Government would take steps to prevent this problem from recurring in future, I explained that MOF will amend the GST Act to simplify and clarify the rules around when GST should be charged on Government fees.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minster for Finance)
text: Fees in the non-taxable list would include those for applications to confer approval for the conduct of a regulated activity.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minster for Finance)
text: For example, applications for professional licences and their licence renewal fees will be non-taxable, as they confer applicants the right to practise in the regulated profession.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minster for Finance)
text: This would also include the 18 regulatory fees that we are refunding.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minster for Finance)
text: All other fees that are not part of this list will be subject to GST.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minster for Finance)
text: This is provided for under clause 2 of the Bill.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minster for Finance)
text: As part of this change in legislative approach, moving forward, MOF and the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS) will henceforth work closely with agencies to assess their fees instead of allowing self-assessment by agencies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minster for Finance)
text: MOF had earlier reviewed all the regulatory and ancillary fees that currently charge GST and announced in February the refund of GST on 18 fees, where GST was wrongly charged.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minster for Finance)
text: If Parliament approves this Bill, the initial list of non-taxable fees will be published in the Gazette in end-April, when the Bill comes into force.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minster for Finance)
text: MOF will continue to work with agencies to progressively prescribe their regulatory fees in the non-taxable list and we aim to complete this by September 2024.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minster for Finance)
text: All fees that are not prescribed in the non-taxable list, will be subject to GST.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minster for Finance)
text: The first category, which is the vast majority of fees, comprises fees for services provided by the Government, which are clearly subject to GST and are already charged with GST today.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minster for Finance)
text: There is no change in the treatment of these fees.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minster for Finance)
text: Examples are fees for the rental of public sports facilities which I mentioned earlier.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minster for Finance)
text: The second category comprises fees that are charged with GST today, but where there has been inconsistency in the interpretation of the law by agencies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minster for Finance)
text: Agencies may charge fees for examinations that an individual must undertake prior to being licensed as a practising professional in a regulated industry.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minster for Finance)
text: Some agencies have assessed such examination fees as taxable, whereas others have not – arising from differing interpretations of the GST Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minster for Finance)
text: Based on our policy intent, as I have clarified above, such examination fees should attract GST.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minster for Finance)
text: Only the eventual licence fee that confers applicants with the regulatory approval to practise should not be taxable.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minster for Finance)
text: The charging of GST on these fees is in line with our clarified policy intent but is susceptible to legal challenge under the current GST Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minster for Finance)
text: Hence, for agencies that have been charging GST on such fees, we will validate these past GST collections, should they not have been made in accordance with the current GST Act, to ensure consistency between the legal position and the clarified policy intent, which is to subject these fees to GST.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minster for Finance)
text: Clause 4 of the Bill provides for this.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minster for Finance)
text: For these two categories of fees, there is no change to the status quo.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minster for Finance)
text: These fees are already charged with GST today and will continue to be charged with GST.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minster for Finance)
text: The third category are fees that are not charged with GST today, but should be charged with GST moving forward, based on our clarified policy intent.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minster for Finance)
text: These include examination fees, which some agencies are currently not charging GST.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minster for Finance)
text: Other examples include inspection fees prior to the licensing and conduct of certain business operations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minster for Finance)
text: We estimate that there are more than a hundred such examination and inspection-related fees.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minster for Finance)
text: Hence, all affected fees will not increase immediately as a result of the amendments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minster for Finance)
text: This will provide greater clarity and certainty to everyone on the GST treatment for Government fees.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding this, the Minister for Finance has the power to disapply the provisions of the GST Act to certain prescribed taxable supplies made by public agencies.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: So, to recap, these were regulatory fees identified to have been charged with GST wrongly and which needed to be refunded.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: To summarise, while clause 4 validates past GST charges on regulatory fees, the specific supplies set out in the Schedule are not shielded by the validation clause.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Primarily, what is the purpose of the validation clause and why has it been included?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Following the Government's internal review last November, which identified inconsistencies in the application of GST on certain Government fees, why is there a need to deem that all previously collected GST in relation to regulatory fees has, in fact, been validly imposed?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The new provision also states that no legal proceedings may be instituted outside of the transactions referred to in the Schedule.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: As MOF has itself mentioned, over 5,000 different types of fees are charged by Government agencies and accordingly, is it possible that other erroneous transactions could have taken place in the past?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: And if so, what recourse will there be for persons affected?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: If this possibility exists, is it then appropriate to retrospectively validate these errors and limit the availability of legal remedies?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Generally speaking, where a GST-registered person wrongly collects an amount of GST with no reasonable excuse or through negligence, that person would have committed an offence and this is one which is punishable by a fine, or prison term or both.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The Comptroller of GST has the power to consider the circumstances of each case.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: But the fact remains that GST-registered persons are held to a high bar when it comes to the wrongful collection of the tax.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: While these two kinds of situations are not exactly the same, the main principle that we can take away is that the wrongful or mistaken collection of GST is indeed a very serious matter.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: As the Minister has explained previously, each Government agency, like any GST-registered business, has to assess whether its fees should be GST-chargeable whenever a fee is introduced or revised.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Agencies did so based on the law, with guidance from MOF and IRAS, but the GST Act is also a complex piece of legislation.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This is understandable and it is laudable that the Government has not shied away from making tough decisions about being transparent whenever errors are made.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: As the Minister has said, the new proposed amendments aim to clarify GST treatment for regulatory and non-regulatory fees moving forward.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: To be clear, I do believe this a is a good development that will minimise errors in interpretation moving forward.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: That being said, I would be grateful if the Minister could share the intentions and thought process behind the inclusion of the validation clause at clause 4 of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: She asked about the purpose of validation clause and whether there were other erroneous transactions in the past.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The charging of GST on these fees is consistent with our policy intent as clarified, but is susceptible to legal challenge under the current GST Act.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We are, therefore, validating the past collections of GST on these fees to clarify the policy intent and legal position should they not have been made in accordance with the current GST Act.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For the 18 fees where the collection of GST was not consistent with our policy intent, we are refunding the GST collected to affected stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As Ms Usha has noted, the GST Act is indeed a complex piece of legislation.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Interpretation and application by agencies on the ground can be challenging.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is why we have proposed the amendments in this Bill to ensure consistency in the policy intent, legal basis and agencies' practices relating to collections of GST on Government fees.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and I will take the Chair at 2.05 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 1.49 pm until 2.05 pm.
